title: About Aditya
text:
I’m Aditya Arya, a junior at Claremont McKenna College. This website presents my work for Foundations of Data Science in R.
The Data Viz menu contains two TidyTuesday analyses: income inequality and Big Tech stock prices. Each page shows the data source, R code, graph, and interpretation.
You can find the website’s files in the GitHub repository.

title: Cool, Cool, Cool: Brooklyn Nine-Nine
text:
For this project, I wanted to find out how often “cool” appears in Brooklyn Nine-Nine, especially when it turns into “cool, cool, cool.” I also wanted to see how this changes across seasons.
I count each “cool” and each repeated sequence separately. So “cool, cool, cool, cool” counts as four mentions of the word and one sequence. I use the available transcripts, which do not tell me who is speaking.

title: Cool, Cool, Cool: Brooklyn Nine-Nine
text:
How often does the word “cool” appear in Brooklyn Nine-Nine transcripts, and how often is it repeated three or more times in a row? Does the frequency change across seasons?
This analysis counts the word itself and repeated sequences separately. For example, “cool, cool, cool, cool” contributes four word occurrences but one repeated sequence. The question is about the available transcripts, which do not identify who is speaking.

title: Cool, Cool, Cool: Brooklyn Nine-Nine
text:
Data and coverage
The data come from Atharva Naik’s Brooklyn Nine-Nine dataset, which credits SubsLikeScript as its transcript source. The original JSON files are stored in this website’s repository under data/brooklyn99. Each contains a list of transcript blocks.
There are 134 files across seasons 1–7. Some episodes are missing, and season 8 is absent. The file season-4/episode-11-DUPE.json is excluded because its episode identification is ambiguous; it is also much longer than the other season 4 files. The raw file is preserved. This leaves 133 files for analysis, rather than a complete record of the show.
The code below loads each file, extracts season and episode numbers from its path, and cleans the text. It removes identified subtitle credits, converts uppercase letters to lowercase, and standardizes spaces. Joining the blocks allows a repeated sequence to continue across a subtitle line break. Repeated dialogue is kept, since repetition is the subject of the analysis.


Show R code
library(tidyverse)

files <- list.files(
  "data/brooklyn99", pattern = "\\.json$",
  recursive = TRUE, full.names = TRUE
)

transcripts <- tibble(source_file = files) |>
  mutate(
    text = map_chr(source_file, function(file) {
      lines <- jsonlite::fromJSON(file)
      lines <- lines[!str_detect(
        lines, regex("synced.*(chamallow|moustafa|maxpayne)", ignore_case = TRUE)
      )]
      str_c(lines, collapse = " ")
    }),
    season = as.integer(str_extract(source_file, "(?<=season-)\\d+")),
    episode = as.integer(str_extract(source_file, "(?<=episode-)\\d+")),
    title = str_remove(basename(source_file), "^episode-\\d+-"),
    title = str_remove(title, "\\.json$"),
    title = str_replace_all(title, "_", " ")
  )

episodes <- transcripts |>
  filter(!str_detect(source_file, "DUPE")) |>
  mutate(
    text = str_replace_all(text, fixed("Ripped By mstoll"), ""),
    text = str_replace_all(text, fixed("&"), "&"),
    text = str_replace_all(text, ">", ""),
    text = str_squish(str_to_lower(text))
  )

title: Cool, Cool, Cool: Brooklyn Nine-Nine
text:
Counting rules

Count “cool” as a whole word, regardless of capitalization. Words such as “cooler,” “coolest,” and “cooling” do not count.
A repeated sequence contains at least three consecutive occurrences of “cool,” separated only by punctuation or spaces. Commas, periods, hyphens, and subtitle line breaks can separate them.
Count the longest continuous sequence once. A sequence of six does not become two sequences of three.
Include every textual use of “cool,” including quoted repetitions and phrases such as “not cool.” These are word counts, not a classification of the speaker’s meaning.

The cool_pattern uses a negative lookbehind and a negative lookahead to prevent matching “cool” inside a longer word. In run_pattern, {2,} requires at least two additional occurrences after the first. The code also counts transcript words as letter/number groups, allowing internal apostrophes. This supplies a consistent denominator for comparing seasons.


Show R code
cool_pattern <- "(?<!\\w)cool(?!\\w)"
run_pattern <- "(?<!\\w)cool(?!\\w)(?:[\\s\\p{P}]+cool(?!\\w)){2,}"
word_pattern <- "\\b\\w+(?:['’]\\w+)*\\b"

episodes <- episodes |>
  mutate(
    words = str_count(text, word_pattern),
    cool_mentions = str_count(text, cool_pattern),
    runs = str_extract_all(text, run_pattern),
    repeated_sequences = lengths(runs)
  )

runs <- episodes |>
  select(season, episode, title, runs) |>
  unnest_longer(runs, values_to = "sequence") |>
  mutate(run_length = str_count(sequence, cool_pattern))


Across the retained files, there are 529 occurrences of “cool” and 22 repeated sequences. Those sequences contain 139 of the word occurrences, or about 26.3% of the total. The remaining occurrences can be single uses or pairs; they are not necessarily all isolated uses.

title: Cool, Cool, Cool: Brooklyn Nine-Nine
section: Does the frequency change by season?
text:
Does the frequency change by season?
Seasons have different numbers of available transcripts and different amounts of dialogue. To account for this, each rate below divides the season’s total count by its total transcript words and multiplies by 1,000. These are pooled season rates, not averages of individual episode rates.


Show R code
season_summary <- episodes |>
  group_by(season) |>
  summarise(
    transcript_files = n(),
    words = sum(words),
    cool_mentions = sum(cool_mentions),
    repeated_sequences = sum(repeated_sequences),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    cool_per_1000 = 1000 * cool_mentions / words,
    runs_per_1000 = 1000 * repeated_sequences / words
  )

season_plot_data <- season_summary |>
  select(season, cool_per_1000, runs_per_1000) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(cool_per_1000, runs_per_1000),
    names_to = "measure", values_to = "rate"
  ) |>
  mutate(measure = recode(
    measure,
    cool_per_1000 = "All occurrences of cool",
    runs_per_1000 = "Sequences of 3+ cools"
  ))


ggplot(season_plot_data, aes(x = season, y = rate)) +
  geom_line(color = "#245680", linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(color = "#245680", size = 2.5) +
  facet_wrap(~ measure, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:7) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, NA)) +
  labs(
    title = "How often does cool appear across seasons?",
    subtitle = "Counts per 1,000 words in the available transcripts",
    x = "Season",
    y = "Occurrences or sequences per 1,000 words",
    caption = "Source: Atharva Naik / SubsLikeScript; 133 retained files. Panels use different y-axis scales."
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)









Season 6 has the highest overall rate, at about 1.47 occurrences per 1,000 words. Season 1 has 54 occurrences but no sequences of three or more under this definition. Repeated sequences appear in the available files from season 2 onward.
The pattern does not rise steadily every season. It also should not be interpreted as a definitive trend for the whole show: missing episodes could change the season comparisons, particularly season 6, which has only 11 files in this dataset.

title: Cool, Cool, Cool: Brooklyn Nine-Nine
section: How long are the repeated sequences?
text:
How long are the repeated sequences?


Show R code
run_summary <- runs |>
  count(run_length, name = "sequences")

top_episodes <- episodes |>
  arrange(season, episode) |>
  slice_max(cool_mentions, n = 10, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  mutate(episode_label = str_c("S", season, " E", episode, ": ", title))

ggplot(run_summary, aes(x = factor(run_length), y = sequences)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#245680", width = 0.7) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, max(run_summary$sequences), by = 1)) +
  labs(
    title = "Some cool sequences continue well beyond three repetitions",
    subtitle = "Each continuous sequence of 3+ is counted once",
    x = "Number of cool occurrences in a sequence",
    y = "Number of sequences",
    caption = "Source: Atharva Naik / SubsLikeScript; only observed sequence lengths are shown."
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)









The most common length is 3, appearing 7 times. The longest detected sequence contains 29 occurrences in season 4, episode 22, listed as “Crime Punishment” in the source filename. The original blocks were checked: the repetition continues across several blocks, which is why the analysis joins them before matching.
That long sequence follows from the stated counting rule. It is not a verified count of one character’s delivery or proof that every repetition was transcribed accurately. For example, a quoted repetition by another character still counts, and adjacent uses by different speakers cannot be separated reliably with these data.

title: Cool, Cool, Cool: Brooklyn Nine-Nine
section: Which episodes have the most cool occurrences?
text:
Which episodes have the most cool occurrences?
This graph ranks files by total word occurrences, including occurrences inside repeated sequences. It shows which available episode transcripts contribute most to the total; longer transcripts have more opportunities to contain the word. Episode titles are taken from the dataset filenames.


Show R code
ggplot(
  top_episodes,
  aes(x = cool_mentions, y = fct_reorder(episode_label, cool_mentions))
) +
  geom_col(fill = "#245680", width = 0.7) +
  labs(
    title = "The ten episode files with the most cool occurrences",
    x = "Occurrences of the whole word cool",
    y = "Episode file (season and episode)",
    caption = "Source: Atharva Naik / SubsLikeScript; total counts, not rates."
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)









Season 4, episode 22 leads with 31 occurrences, largely because of its long repeated sequence. This shows how a single passage can drive an episode’s count. The next two files, “The Crime Scene” and “Casecation,” each contain 16 occurrences.

title: Cool, Cool, Cool: Brooklyn Nine-Nine
text:
What this tells us
The available transcripts show both ordinary uses of “cool” and longer repeated sequences. Repetition accounts for about a quarter of all occurrences, so it contributes meaningfully to the word’s overall frequency. Comparing normalized rates adds context to the raw totals, while the episode ranking shows how individual passages can influence them.
These results describe this incomplete transcript collection. They do not establish who says the word most, the emotional meaning of each use, or the total number of times “cool” is spoken in the complete show. The source was already scraped and cleaned before this analysis, so omissions, combined blocks, and transcription errors remain possible.

title: Income Inequality Before and After Taxes
text:
How do pre-tax and post-tax income inequality compare across countries in 2020?
The Gini coefficient measures income inequality from 0 to 1. Higher numbers mean more inequality. The data come from TidyTuesday’s income inequality dataset.
In the file used here, each row is a country (or region) in one year. I use Year to select 2020, gini_mi_eq for the pre-tax measure, and gini_dhi_eq for the post-tax measure. Both measures adjust income for household size. “Pre-tax” and “post-tax” are short names for income before and after taxes and benefits.

library(tidyverse)

income_inequality <- read_csv(
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2025/2025-08-05/income_inequality_processed.csv"
)

title: Income Inequality Before and After Taxes
text:
How do pre-tax and post-tax income inequality compare across countries in 2020?
The Gini coefficient measures income inequality from 0 to 1. Higher numbers mean more inequality. The data come from TidyTuesday’s income inequality dataset.
In the file used here, each row is a country (or region) in one year. I use Year to select 2020, gini_mi_eq for the pre-tax measure, and gini_dhi_eq for the post-tax measure. Both measures adjust income for household size. “Pre-tax” and “post-tax” are short names for income before and after taxes and benefits.

library(tidyverse)

income_inequality <- read_csv(
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2025/2025-08-05/income_inequality_processed.csv"
)

title: Income Inequality Before and After Taxes
text:
Choose the observations
I use 2020 because the dataset has both Gini measures for 19 countries in that year. There are 31 rows for 2020; 12 have no pre-tax Gini value, while none are missing the post-tax value. Gini values run from 0 to 1, so filtering for values at least 0 keeps the recorded values and drops the missing rows. This means the graph compares only countries with both values available, not every country in the world.

inequality_2020 <- income_inequality |>
  filter(
    Year == 2020,
    gini_mi_eq >= 0,
    gini_dhi_eq >= 0
  )

title: Income Inequality Before and After Taxes
text:
Make a graph
Each point represents one country. The horizontal position shows its pre-tax Gini coefficient, and the vertical position shows its post-tax Gini coefficient.

ggplot(inequality_2020, aes(x = gini_mi_eq, y = gini_dhi_eq)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    title = "Income inequality before and after taxes in 2020",
    x = "Pre-tax Gini coefficient",
    y = "Post-tax Gini coefficient",
    caption = "Source: Our World in Data via TidyTuesday"
  )








In this dataset, the post-tax Gini coefficient is lower than the pre-tax coefficient for all 19 countries shown. This is a comparison of the measures, not proof that a particular policy caused the difference.

title: Income Inequality Before and After Taxes
text:
Sources

TidyTuesday. (2025, August 5). Income Inequality Before and After Taxes (data and variable descriptions).
Hasell, J. (2023, July 3). Income inequality before and after taxes: how much do countries redistribute income? Our World in Data (original data processing and explanation).
Luxembourg Income Study. (2025). LIS Database (underlying household-income data, as credited by TidyTuesday and Our World in Data).

title: Big Tech Stock Prices in 2022
text:
How did Apple and Microsoft’s adjusted closing stock prices change during 2022?
This dataset was shared by TidyTuesday on February 7, 2023. It contains daily stock prices for 14 technology companies. Each row is one company’s stock on one trading day. For this graph, I use stock_symbol to choose Apple (AAPL) and Microsoft (MSFT), date for the horizontal axis, and adj_close for the vertical axis. Adjusted close accounts for stock splits and dividends.

library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)

big_tech_stock_prices <- read_csv(
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2023/2023-02-07/big_tech_stock_prices.csv"
)

title: Big Tech Stock Prices in 2022
text:
How did Apple and Microsoft’s adjusted closing stock prices change during 2022?
This dataset was shared by TidyTuesday on February 7, 2023. It contains daily stock prices for 14 technology companies. Each row is one company’s stock on one trading day. For this graph, I use stock_symbol to choose Apple (AAPL) and Microsoft (MSFT), date for the horizontal axis, and adj_close for the vertical axis. Adjusted close accounts for stock splits and dividends.

library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)

big_tech_stock_prices <- read_csv(
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2023/2023-02-07/big_tech_stock_prices.csv"
)

title: Big Tech Stock Prices in 2022
text:
Choose the observations
I keep Apple and Microsoft trading days in 2022. There are 250 rows for each company in this period, and none of these rows is missing a date or adjusted closing price. Non-trading days are not included in the dataset.

stocks_2022 <- big_tech_stock_prices |>
  filter(
    stock_symbol == "AAPL" | stock_symbol == "MSFT",
    date >= ymd("2022-01-01"),
    date <= ymd("2022-12-31")
  )

title: Big Tech Stock Prices in 2022
text:
Make a graph
Each line shows one company’s adjusted closing price per share on the trading days in the dataset.

ggplot(stocks_2022, aes(x = date, y = adj_close, color = stock_symbol)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(
    title = "Apple and Microsoft stock prices in 2022",
    x = "Date",
    y = "Adjusted closing price (US dollars per share)",
    color = "Company",
    caption = "Source: Yahoo Finance via Evan Gower and TidyTuesday"
  )








Apple and Microsoft’s stock prices often moved in similar directions during 2022, but this graph alone doesn’t show why. Both lines also end lower than they begin. These are prices per share, not the total values of the companies.

title: Big Tech Stock Prices in 2022
text:
Sources

TidyTuesday. (2023, February 7). Big Tech Stock Prices (dataset and variable descriptions).
Gower, E. Big Tech Stock Prices. Kaggle (the dataset TidyTuesday used).
Yahoo Finance. Historical market data (original stock-price source, as credited by TidyTuesday).

Read the analysis →

title: Aditya Arya | Data Science
text:
About this project
This site is made with Quarto and R for Foundations of Data Science. The source files, including the .qmd pages and rendered website, are in the GitHub repository.

title: Cool, Cool, Cool: Brooklyn Nine-Nine
text:
For this project, I wanted to find out how often “cool” appears in Brooklyn Nine-Nine, especially when it turns into “cool, cool, cool.” I also wanted to see how this changes across seasons.
I count each “cool” and each repeated sequence separately. So “cool, cool, cool, cool” counts as four mentions of the word and one sequence. I use the available transcripts, which do not tell me who is speaking.

title: Cool, Cool, Cool: Brooklyn Nine-Nine
text:
Getting the data ready
The data come from Atharva Naik’s Brooklyn Nine-Nine dataset. He collected the transcripts from SubsLikeScript. The original files are saved in data/brooklyn99 in this website’s GitHub repository. Each file contains pieces of an episode’s transcript.
The dataset has 134 files from seasons 1–7, but some episodes are missing and there is no season 8. I leave out season-4/episode-11-DUPE.json because it is unclear which episode it represents. It is also much longer than the other season 4 files. I keep the original file in the data folder, but leaving it out of the analysis gives me 133 transcript files to work with.
First, I load the files and get the season and episode numbers from their names. Then I remove the subtitle credits I identified, make the text lowercase, and clean up extra spaces. I join the pieces of each transcript so a line break does not cut off a repeated “cool.” I keep repeated dialogue because that is what I am trying to count.


Show R code
library(tidyverse)

files <- list.files(
  "data/brooklyn99", pattern = "\\.json$",
  recursive = TRUE, full.names = TRUE
)

transcripts <- tibble(source_file = files) |>
  mutate(
    text = map_chr(source_file, function(file) {
      lines <- jsonlite::fromJSON(file)
      lines <- lines[!str_detect(
        lines, regex("synced.*(chamallow|moustafa|maxpayne)", ignore_case = TRUE)
      )]
      str_c(lines, collapse = " ")
    }),
    season = as.integer(str_extract(source_file, "(?<=season-)\\d+")),
    episode = as.integer(str_extract(source_file, "(?<=episode-)\\d+")),
    title = str_remove(basename(source_file), "^episode-\\d+-"),
    title = str_remove(title, "\\.json$"),
    title = str_replace_all(title, "_", " ")
  )

episodes <- transcripts |>
  filter(!str_detect(source_file, "DUPE")) |>
  mutate(
    text = str_replace_all(text, fixed("Ripped By mstoll"), ""),
    text = str_replace_all(text, fixed("&"), "&"),
    text = str_replace_all(text, ">", ""),
    text = str_squish(str_to_lower(text))
  )

title: Cool, Cool, Cool: Brooklyn Nine-Nine
text:
What counts as “cool”?

“Cool” and “cool” both count. “Cooler,” “coolest,” and “cooling” do not.
A repeated sequence needs three or more “cool”s in a row. Spaces, commas, periods, hyphens, and line breaks can come between them.
Six “cool”s in a row count as one sequence, not two sequences of three.
I count “cool” even in “not cool” or when someone quotes another person. I am counting the words, not deciding what they mean in each scene.

The lookbehind and lookahead in cool_pattern check that “cool” is not part of a longer word. In run_pattern, {2,} looks for at least two more “cool”s after the first one. I also count the words in each transcript so I can compare seasons. For this count, a word is a group of letters or numbers, and apostrophes inside a word are allowed.


Show R code
cool_pattern <- "(?<!\\w)cool(?!\\w)"
run_pattern <- "(?<!\\w)cool(?!\\w)(?:[\\s\\p{P}]+cool(?!\\w)){2,}"
word_pattern <- "\\b\\w+(?:['’]\\w+)*\\b"

episodes <- episodes |>
  mutate(
    words = str_count(text, word_pattern),
    cool_mentions = str_count(text, cool_pattern),
    runs = str_extract_all(text, run_pattern),
    repeated_sequences = lengths(runs)
  )

runs <- episodes |>
  select(season, episode, title, runs) |>
  unnest_longer(runs, values_to = "sequence") |>
  mutate(run_length = str_count(sequence, cool_pattern))


In these files, “cool” appears 529 times, with 22 sequences of three or more. Those sequences account for 139 mentions, or 26.3% of the total. The other mentions include both single uses and pairs.

title: Cool, Cool, Cool: Brooklyn Nine-Nine
text:
Does it change by season?
Some seasons have more transcripts than others, so comparing only the totals would give them more chances to come out on top. Instead, I compare counts per 1,000 transcript words. I calculate this by dividing each season’s total count by its total words and multiplying by 1,000. I use the season totals rather than averaging the rates for separate episodes.


Show R code
season_summary <- episodes |>
  group_by(season) |>
  summarise(
    transcript_files = n(),
    words = sum(words),
    cool_mentions = sum(cool_mentions),
    repeated_sequences = sum(repeated_sequences),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    cool_per_1000 = 1000 * cool_mentions / words,
    runs_per_1000 = 1000 * repeated_sequences / words
  )

season_plot_data <- season_summary |>
  select(season, cool_per_1000, runs_per_1000) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(cool_per_1000, runs_per_1000),
    names_to = "measure", values_to = "rate"
  ) |>
  mutate(measure = recode(
    measure,
    cool_per_1000 = "All occurrences of cool",
    runs_per_1000 = "Sequences of 3+ cools"
  ))


ggplot(season_plot_data, aes(x = season, y = rate)) +
  geom_line(color = "#245680", linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(color = "#245680", size = 2.5) +
  facet_wrap(~ measure, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:7) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, NA)) +
  labs(
    title = "How often does cool appear across seasons?",
    subtitle = "Counts per 1,000 words in the available transcripts",
    x = "Season",
    y = "Occurrences or sequences per 1,000 words",
    caption = "Source: Atharva Naik / SubsLikeScript; 133 retained files. Panels use different y-axis scales."
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)









Season 6 has the highest rate, with about 1.47 “cool”s per 1,000 words. Season 1 has 54 mentions, but none are in a sequence of three or more. In this dataset, those sequences start appearing in season 2.
The graph goes up and down, so “cool” does not simply become more common every season. Also, season 6 only has 11 files here. The missing episodes could change how the seasons compare, so I would not treat this as the final result for the whole show.

title: Cool, Cool, Cool: Brooklyn Nine-Nine
section: How many “cool”s are said in a row?
text:
How many “cool”s are said in a row?


Show R code
run_summary <- runs |>
  count(run_length, name = "sequences")

top_episodes <- episodes |>
  arrange(season, episode) |>
  slice_max(cool_mentions, n = 10, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  mutate(episode_label = str_c("S", season, " E", episode, ": ", title))

ggplot(run_summary, aes(x = factor(run_length), y = sequences)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#245680", width = 0.7) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, max(run_summary$sequences), by = 1)) +
  labs(
    title = "Some cool sequences continue well beyond three repetitions",
    subtitle = "Each continuous sequence of 3+ is counted once",
    x = "Number of cool occurrences in a sequence",
    y = "Number of sequences",
    caption = "Source: Atharva Naik / SubsLikeScript; only observed sequence lengths are shown."
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)









The most common sequence has 3 “cool”s in a row. There are 7 of these. The longest has 29 and comes from season 4, episode 22, labeled “Crime Punishment” in the filename. In the original file, that repetition runs across several transcript blocks. Joining them keeps it as one sequence.
That does not necessarily mean one character says all of those “cool”s. The transcripts do not label speakers, so the count can join consecutive uses by different people. It also includes someone quoting the phrase. The result depends on the counting rule and on how accurately the dialogue was transcribed.

title: Cool, Cool, Cool: Brooklyn Nine-Nine
text:
Which episodes use “cool” the most?
For this graph, I rank the episode files by their total “cool” counts. This includes mentions inside repeated sequences. Unlike the season graph, these are raw totals, so longer transcripts have more chances to include the word. The episode names come from the filenames.


Show R code
ggplot(
  top_episodes,
  aes(x = cool_mentions, y = fct_reorder(episode_label, cool_mentions))
) +
  geom_col(fill = "#245680", width = 0.7) +
  labs(
    title = "The ten episode files with the most cool occurrences",
    x = "Occurrences of the whole word cool",
    y = "Episode file (season and episode)",
    caption = "Source: Atharva Naik / SubsLikeScript; total counts, not rates."
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)









Season 4, episode 22 comes first with 31 mentions. Most come from its long repeated sequence, so one part of the episode explains a lot of its total. “The Crime Scene” and “Casecation” are next, with 16 mentions each.

title: Cool, Cool, Cool: Brooklyn Nine-Nine
text:
What I found
The repeated “cool, cool, cool” sequences make up about a quarter of all the “cool” mentions in these files. So they explain a noticeable part of the total, even though there are only 22 sequences. The season graph shows how often the word appears relative to the amount of dialogue, while the episode graph shows how one long repetition can push an episode to the top.
This is still an incomplete dataset, so I cannot say how many times “cool” is said in the entire show or who says it most. The transcripts were already collected and cleaned before this project, and they may have mistakes or missing dialogue. My results describe the files available here.

title: Adelie Penguin Flipper Lengths on Two Islands
text:
Do Adelie penguins on Biscoe and Dream islands have different average flipper lengths?
For this project, I compare flipper lengths on the two islands using the Palmer penguins dataset. I use only Adelie penguins so that differences between species do not affect the comparison. I first graph the measurements and calculate the difference in the two averages. Then I shuffle the measurements 10,000 times to see how often a difference at least this large comes up by chance under the null hypothesis.
The data come from the palmerpenguins package. Dr. Kristen Gorman and the Palmer Station Long Term Ecological Research program collected the original measurements in Antarctica during 2007–2009. Each row is one penguin. I use species to choose Adelie penguins, island to choose Biscoe and Dream, and flipper_length_mm for flipper length in millimeters.

library(tidyverse)

penguins <- read_csv("data/penguins.csv")

title: Adelie Penguin Flipper Lengths on Two Islands
text:
Conclusion
I compared the flipper lengths of 100 Adelie penguins from Biscoe and Dream islands and found that the Dream average was 0.94 mm higher. I shuffled the measurements 10,000 times and got an estimated p-value of 0.49, so I did not reject the null hypothesis at the 5% level. This result does not provide strong evidence that the population means differ, but it does not prove that they are equal. Any broader conclusion is limited to Adelie penguins represented by these sampled colonies during 2007–2009, rather than all penguins.

title: Adelie Penguin Flipper Lengths on Two Islands
text:
Do Adelie penguins on Biscoe and Dream islands have different average flipper lengths?
For this project, I compare flipper lengths on the two islands using the Palmer penguins dataset. I use only Adelie penguins so that differences between species do not affect the comparison. I first graph the measurements and calculate the difference in the two averages. Then I shuffle the measurements 10,000 times to see how often a difference at least this large comes up by chance under the null hypothesis.
The data come from the palmerpenguins package. Dr. Kristen Gorman and the Palmer Station Long Term Ecological Research program collected the original measurements in Antarctica during 2007–2009. Each row is one penguin. I use species to choose Adelie penguins, island to choose Biscoe and Dream, and flipper_length_mm for flipper length in millimeters.

library(tidyverse)

penguins <- read_csv("data/penguins.csv")

title: Adelie Penguin Flipper Lengths on Two Islands
text:
Choose the observations
I keep Adelie penguins from Biscoe and Dream islands with a recorded flipper length. The dataset contains 44 Adelie penguins from Biscoe and 56 from Dream. None of these 100 penguins is missing a flipper length, so the missing-value filter does not remove any of them. I use the package’s penguins.csv file, saved in this website’s data folder so the analysis can run from the repository.

adelie <- penguins |>
  filter(
    species == "Adelie",
    island == "Biscoe" | island == "Dream",
    !is.na(flipper_length_mm)
  )

title: Adelie Penguin Flipper Lengths on Two Islands
text:
Make a graph
Each box shows the middle half of the flipper lengths on one island. The line inside the box marks the median.

ggplot(adelie, aes(x = island, y = flipper_length_mm)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(
    title = "Adelie penguin flipper lengths on two islands",
    x = "Island",
    y = "Flipper length (mm)",
    caption = "Source: Palmer Station LTER via palmerpenguins, 2007–2009"
  )








The flipper lengths overlap substantially across the two islands. The medians are also close together. This graph shows the spread of the measurements, but I use the difference in means for the test below.

title: Adelie Penguin Flipper Lengths on Two Islands
Adelie Penguin Flipper Lengths on Two Islands
Adelie Penguin Flipper Lengths on Two Islands
text:
Graph the simulated differences
Each bar shows how many simulated differences fall in that interval. The red lines mark the positive and negative values that are the same distance from zero as the observed difference.

ggplot(simulation, aes(x = difference)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = c(-observed_difference, observed_difference),
    color = "red"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Differences in mean flipper length after shuffling",
    subtitle = "Red lines mark the observed difference in each direction",
    x = "Dream mean minus Biscoe mean (mm)",
    y = "Number of simulations",
    caption = "10,000 shuffles of the Palmer penguin measurements"
  )








The simulated differences are centered near zero. The red lines sit within the main part of the distribution, and about half the shuffles produce differences at least this far from zero. This suggests that the observed difference is not unusual under the null hypothesis.

title: Adelie Penguin Flipper Lengths on Two Islands
text:
Find the p-value
For a two-sided test, I count differences at least as far from zero as the observed difference, in either direction. abs() gives the distance from zero. Dividing this count by 10,000 gives the estimated p-value.

extreme_count <- sum(
  abs(null_differences) >= abs(observed_difference)
)

p_value <- extreme_count / length(null_differences)

In this simulation, 4915 out of 10,000 shuffles produced a difference at least as large in absolute value as the observed difference. The estimated p-value is 0.49. This is the proportion of results at least this extreme under the null model, not the probability that the null hypothesis is true.

Sources

Horst, A. M., Hill, A. P., & Gorman, K. B. (2020). palmerpenguins: Palmer Archipelago (Antarctica) penguin data (the package’s penguins.csv file used here).
Palmer Station Antarctica LTER & K. Gorman (2020). Adelie penguin measurements, 2007–2009 (original data).
Gorman, K. B., Williams, T. D., & Fraser, W. R. (2014). Ecological sexual dimorphism and environmental variability within a community of Antarctic penguins. PLOS ONE, 9(3), e90081 (original study).
Hardin, J. DS002R notes: Permutation tests (examples of shuffling measurements and repeating a simulation).

title: Adelie Penguin Flipper Lengths on Two Islands
text:
Assumptions and limits
The test assumes that the measurements can be treated as independent and shuffled between groups under the null hypothesis. This simple comparison does not account for sex, year, or possible dependence between birds in the sample. The data are observational, so the comparison also cannot show that living on an island causes a change in flipper length.
